```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
from scipy import stats
import json, pathlib
from IPython.display import HTML, display

rng = np.random.default_rng(20260824)

C = {
    "blue":   "#2c6e9b",
    "orange": "#d1743a",
    "green":  "#4f8f63",
    "red":    "#b5483d",
    "grey":   "#9aa3ab",
    "dark":   "#2c4a63",
}

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 130,
    "font.size": 9,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

WIDGET_COLORS = {
    "blue": C["blue"], "dark": C["dark"], "red": C["red"],
    "green": C["green"], "grey": C["grey"],
    "grid": "#ccd4db", "axis": "#9aa4ad", "tick": "#3f4850",
}


def correlated_X(N, p, rng):
    """N units, p covariates, with a non-trivial correlation structure."""
    A = rng.normal(size=(p, p))
    Sig = A @ A.T + np.eye(p)
    d = np.sqrt(np.diag(Sig))
    Sig = Sig / np.outer(d, d)
    return rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(p), Sig, size=N)


def pair_distances(X):
    """Squared Mahalanobis distance between every pair of units.

    Whitening first turns the quadratic form into a plain squared Euclidean
    distance, which lets the whole matrix be built in one vectorised step.
    """
    S = np.cov(X, rowvar=False, bias=True)
    Si = np.linalg.inv(S)
    Z = X @ np.linalg.cholesky(Si).T.T
    return ((Z[:, None, :] - Z[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1), Si, S


def whiten(X):
    """Rescale X so its sample covariance is exactly the identity.

    D^2 is unchanged by any linear rescaling of the covariates, so this alters
    no distance. It only makes the picture honest: with S = I the Mahalanobis
    distance is the plain straight-line distance, and a line that looks twice
    as long really is.
    """
    Xc = X - X.mean(0)
    S = np.cov(Xc, rowvar=False, bias=True)
    return Xc @ np.linalg.inv(np.linalg.cholesky(S)).T


def optimal_pairs(d2):
    """Minimum-weight perfect matching on the complete graph (blossom)."""
    N = d2.shape[0]
    G = nx.Graph()
    for i in range(N):
        for j in range(i + 1, N):
            G.add_edge(i, j, weight=d2[i, j])
    return np.array([tuple(e) for e in nx.min_weight_matching(G)])


def greedy_pairs(d2):
    """Repeatedly take the closest remaining available pair."""
    N = d2.shape[0]
    d = d2.astype(float).copy()
    np.fill_diagonal(d, np.inf)
    out = []
    for _ in range(N // 2):
        i, j = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(d), d.shape)
        out.append((int(i), int(j)))
        d[[i, j], :] = np.inf
        d[:, [i, j]] = np.inf
    return np.array(out)


def widget(name, div_id, payload, html):
    """Inline a canvas widget with its data, no CDN and no build step."""
    js = pathlib.Path(name).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    js = js.replace("__ID__", div_id).replace("__DATA__", json.dumps(payload))
    display(HTML(html + "<script>" + js + "</script>"))
```

With a few hundred units, you want a control group and a treatment group that
are as similar to each other as possible before the intervention begins.
[Rerandomization](../rerandomization/) reaches that by discarding splits that
come out badly balanced. Pairwise matching reaches it by construction.
Matching pairs units with similar characteristics, and within each pair a coin
flip decides which unit receives treatment and which serves as its control. So
the two groups are balanced pair by pair, not just on average.

This article asks whether matching beats rerandomization, why pairing needs
solving properly, and how to analyse the experiment afterwards.

## What it does

Closeness between two units is measured with the [Mahalanobis
distance](../mahalanobis-distance/). With (even) $N$ units and $k$ covariates:

::: {.keybox}
1. Compute the covariate covariance matrix $S$ once, from all $N$ units.
2. For every pair of units $i$ and $j$, compute the squared distance between
   them:
   $$ D^2(i,j) \;=\; (x_i - x_j)^{\!\top} S^{-1} (x_i - x_j). $$
3. Choose the $N/2$ pairs that **minimise the total within-pair distance**,
   subject to covering every unit exactly once.
4. Inside each pair, flip a coin to decide which unit goes to treatment.
:::

We will cover the case where $N$ is odd later in this article.

Step 2 is the same quadratic form as in the Mahalanobis article, applied to
the gap between two units instead of the gap between a unit and the mean.

Step 4 is what keeps this a randomised experiment. Assigning deterministically
inside pairs, say the higher-spending unit always to control, would leave a
single possible split and no basis for a $p$-value, where the coin flips leave
$2^{N/2}$, about $1.6 \times 10^{60}$ at $N = 400$.

## Does it gain more than rerandomization?

Both designs are aiming at the same thing, so the comparison is worth making
directly. The covariates are held fixed throughout: 400 units with four of
them. Two outcomes are built on those covariates, carrying the same total
signal and differing only in how much of it a linear function can reach. Each
design is then run 4,000 times against each outcome. Matching solves the
pairing once and then flips a fresh coin inside every pair, so its 4,000
assignments are all different. The gain is expressed as the sample you would
need under plain randomisation to estimate the treatment effect just as
precisely.

```{python}
#| label: headtohead-setup
#| include: false

N, p, REPS = 400, 4, 4000
rng_h = np.random.default_rng(7)

Xh = correlated_X(N, p, rng_h)
d2h, Sih, _ = pair_distances(Xh)
pairs = optimal_pairs(d2h)
assert len(pairs) == N // 2 and len(set(pairs.ravel())) == N
i0, i1 = pairs[:, 0], pairs[:, 1]
nP = len(pairs)

# ---- three designs, each drawn once and reused for both outcome models -----
T_cr = np.zeros((REPS, N), bool)
for b in range(REPS):
    T_cr[b, rng_h.permutation(N)[: N // 2]] = True

a_thr = stats.chi2.ppf(0.01, p)
T_rr = np.zeros((REPS, N), bool)
for b in range(REPS):
    while True:
        t = np.zeros(N, bool)
        t[rng_h.permutation(N)[: N // 2]] = True
        dbar = Xh[t].mean(0) - Xh[~t].mean(0)
        if (N / 4) * dbar @ Sih @ dbar <= a_thr:
            T_rr[b] = t
            break

coin = rng_h.random((REPS, nP)) < 0.5
T_pm = np.zeros((REPS, N), bool)
T_pm[np.repeat(np.arange(REPS), nP),
     np.where(coin, i0[None, :], i1[None, :]).ravel()] = True

# ---- two outcome models, same covariates, same total signal strength ------
# The models are built to share R^2 overall while differing sharply in how
# much of that signal a linear function of the covariates can reach.
beta = np.array([1.0, 0.6, -0.8, 0.4])
Xi_h = np.column_stack([np.ones(N), Xh])


def make_y(kind, rng):
    if kind == "linear":
        sig = Xh @ beta
    else:
        sig = (2.0 * np.sin(2.2 * Xh[:, 0])
               + 1.5 * (Xh[:, 1] > 0.3) * Xh[:, 2]
               + 0.9 * Xh[:, 0] * Xh[:, 1]
               + 0.8 * Xh[:, 3] ** 2)
    sig = sig / sig.std() * 1.4
    y = sig + rng.normal(0, 1.0, N)
    # The linear share projects the signal, not the outcome, onto X. Projecting
    # the outcome would let OLS fit some of the noise and could push the linear
    # share above the total.
    lin = Xi_h @ np.linalg.lstsq(Xi_h, sig, rcond=None)[0]
    return y, sig.var() / y.var(), lin.var() / y.var()


def est_sd(T, y):
    mt = np.where(T, y[None, :], np.nan)
    mc = np.where(T, np.nan, y[None, :])
    return (np.nanmean(mt, 1) - np.nanmean(mc, 1)).std(ddof=1)


v_a = stats.chi2.cdf(a_thr, p + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_thr, p)

R2 = {}
for kind in ["linear", "nonlinear"]:
    y_k, r2_tot, r2_lin = make_y(kind, np.random.default_rng(3))
    base = est_sd(T_cr, y_k)
    R2[kind] = dict(tot=r2_tot, lin=r2_lin,
                    rr=(est_sd(T_rr, y_k) / base) ** 2,
                    pm=(est_sd(T_pm, y_k) / base) ** 2)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-headtohead
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: 'How much data each design is worth. A bar of two means the experiment estimates the treatment effect as precisely as plain randomisation would on twice the sample. Both outcome models carry the same total signal and differ only in how much of it is linear in the covariates.'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.7))
groups = [("Outcome linear\nin the covariates", "linear"),
          ("Outcome not linear\nin the covariates", "nonlinear")]
ypos = np.arange(len(groups))
hgt = 0.34
# matching first, so the legend runs in the same order as the bars appear
for off, key, lab, col in [(-hgt / 2, "pm", "Pairwise matching", C["blue"]),
                           (+hgt / 2, "rr", "Rerandomization, $p_a$ = 1%",
                            C["orange"])]:
    vals = [1 / R2[k][key] for _, k in groups]
    ax.barh(ypos + off, vals, height=hgt, color=col, label=lab, zorder=3)
    for yy, v in zip(ypos + off, vals):
        ax.text(v + 0.03, yy, f"{v:.1f}×", va="center", fontsize=8.5,
                color="#3f4850")
ax.axvline(1.0, color=C["grey"], lw=1.2, ls="--", zorder=2)
ax.text(1.0, -0.70, "plain randomisation", fontsize=8, color="#6b747c",
        va="bottom", ha="center")
ax.set_yticks(ypos)
ax.set_yticklabels([g for g, _ in groups])
ax.set_xlabel("equivalent sample size, relative to plain randomisation")
ax.set_xlim(0, max(1 / R2[k][m] for _, k in groups for m in ("rr", "pm")) + 0.5)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylim(len(groups) - 0.52, -0.84)      # headroom for the label above
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#e3e8ec", zorder=0)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The two designs behave the same way on a linear outcome and come apart
completely on a non-linear one. The reason is that they are limited by
different quantities. A threshold on $M$ constrains the difference in covariate
*means*, which pins down the linear part of the response and leaves the rest
untouched, so rerandomization is limited by how much of the outcome is linear
in the covariates. That falls from
`{python} f"{R2['linear']['lin']:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['lin']:.2f}"` between the two rows, and the bar
collapses with it.

Matching is limited by the other quantity. The two units in a pair sit close
together in covariate space, so any function of the covariates takes nearly the
same value on each side of the coin flip, whether that function is linear or
not. Both outcome models leave the same share of variance unexplained once any
function is allowed, which is why matching holds up across both rows.

### Is that $R^2$ a fair number?

```{python}
#| label: lalonde
#| include: false

d_ll = pd.read_csv("../../data/lalonde-nsw.csv")
COVS_LL = ["age", "education", "black", "hispanic", "married", "nodegree",
           "re74", "re75"]
X_ll = d_ll[COVS_LL].to_numpy(float)
y_ll = d_ll["re78"].to_numpy(float)
N_ll = len(X_ll) - len(X_ll) % 2
X_ll, y_ll = X_ll[:N_ll], y_ll[:N_ll]
k_ll = X_ll.shape[1]

Xi_ll = np.column_stack([np.ones(N_ll), X_ll])
r2_ll = (Xi_ll @ np.linalg.lstsq(Xi_ll, y_ll, rcond=None)[0]).var() / y_ll.var()

Xc_ll = X_ll - X_ll.mean(0)
Si_ll = np.linalg.pinv(np.cov(Xc_ll, rowvar=False, bias=True))
dif = Xc_ll[:, None, :] - Xc_ll[None, :, :]
d2_ll = np.einsum("ijk,kl,ijl->ij", dif, Si_ll, dif)
p_ll = optimal_pairs(d2_ll)

# Exact design variances, so there is no Monte Carlo error to argue about.
# Pair randomisation: the difference in means is a weighted sum of
# independent within-pair signs. Complete randomisation: 4 s_y^2 / N.
gap_ll = y_ll[p_ll[:, 0]] - y_ll[p_ll[:, 1]]
var_pm_ll = (gap_ll ** 2).sum() / (N_ll // 2) ** 2
var_cr_ll = 4 * y_ll.var(ddof=1) / N_ll
eq_ll = var_cr_ll / var_pm_ll
rho_ll = np.corrcoef(y_ll[p_ll[:, 0]], y_ll[p_ll[:, 1]])[0, 1]
```

It is at the optimistic end, and it was chosen rather than measured, so it is
worth running the same design on real covariates and a real outcome. The
sample here is LaLonde's job-training experiment in Dehejia and Wahba's
version: `{python} f"{N_ll}"` people, `{python} f"{k_ll}"` pre-treatment
covariates, and 1978 earnings as the outcome.

The measured $R^2$ is `{python} f"{r2_ll:.3f}"`. That caps the whole exercise
at `{python} f"{1 / (1 - r2_ll):.2f}"` times the sample, and the optimal
matching delivers `{python} f"{eq_ll:.3f}"` times, about
`{python} f"{100 * (eq_ll - 1) / (1 / (1 - r2_ll) - 1):.0f}"`% of what was
available. On the most studied dataset in the matching literature, pairing
these units is worth roughly
`{python} f"{100 * (eq_ll - 1):.0f}"`% more data.

That is not a failure of the method. It is what the method is worth when the
covariates barely predict the outcome, and age, education and two years of
prior earnings predict 1978 earnings badly. The mechanism is visible in one
number: the within-pair correlation of the outcome is
`{python} f"{rho_ll:+.3f}"`, and pair randomisation only beats complete
randomisation to the extent that correlation is positive. Matching makes pairs
alike in covariates, not in outcomes, and here the two come apart.

The lesson is the ordering. Measure $R^2$ on your own covariates and outcome
first, because it decides whether any of this is worth doing. A design
question that looks like "matching or rerandomization?" is usually settled
before either is reached.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Checking both numbers against theory

The variance ratio under rerandomization is $1 - (1 - v_a)R^2$, with $v_a$ the
shrinkage factor from the [rerandomization article](../rerandomization/) and
$R^2$ the linear one. At $k =$ `{python} f"{p}"` and $p_a = 1\%$,
$v_a =$ `{python} f"{v_a:.3f}"`, so the formula predicts a variance ratio of
`{python} f"{1 - (1 - v_a) * R2['linear']['lin']:.2f}"` for the linear model
against `{python} f"{R2['linear']['rr']:.2f}"` measured, and
`{python} f"{1 - (1 - v_a) * R2['nonlinear']['lin']:.2f}"` for the non-linear
model against `{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['rr']:.2f}"` measured. Splitting the
outcome into its linear fit and the residual shows the mechanism directly:
under rerandomization the variance of the fitted part shrinks by a factor of
about $v_a$, and the variance of the residual part does not move.

For matching, a perfectly matched sample would reduce the variance to
$1 - R^2 =$ `{python} f"{1 - R2['nonlinear']['tot']:.2f}"` here against
`{python} f"{R2['nonlinear']['pm']:.2f}"` achieved. The shortfall is the price
of pairs that are close but not identical.

The two designs also differ in what you can do about a disappointing number.
Tightening the threshold drives $v_a$ towards zero, so rerandomization has a
dial to turn.
:::

Matching has nothing to adjust. The within-pair distances are a property of
the sample, and once the matching is optimal the design is finished. What
limits the result is covariate density, which is why matching improves as $N$
grows and degrades as $k$ grows.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which to reach for

Matching is the safer default when you cannot describe the outcome as roughly
linear in the covariates, and when the sample is small enough that a few
awkward units could land on one side. Rerandomization is the better fit when
the covariates enter the response roughly linearly, when you want a dial you
can tighten, and when the pairing cannot survive to the analysis stage.
:::

## The pairing is an optimisation problem, not a sorting problem

The gain above assumes the pairing is solved properly. This is the step that
goes wrong in practice, and getting it wrong costs most of what the previous
section just measured.

```{python}
#| label: greedy-data
#| include: false

# Whitened to S = I, so the distance being minimised is the length of the line
# on the screen. Whitening changes no distance, only the drawing.
Xd = whiten(np.random.default_rng(11).multivariate_normal(
    np.zeros(2), np.array([[1.0, 0.82], [0.82, 1.0]]), size=40))
d2d, Si_d, S_d = pair_distances(Xd)
assert np.allclose(S_d, np.eye(2), atol=1e-12)
po_d, pg_d = optimal_pairs(d2d), greedy_pairs(d2d)

demo = {
    "mult": (sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in pg_d)
             / sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)),
    "worst": (max(d2d[i, j] for i, j in pg_d)
              / max(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)),
    "last": float(d2d[pg_d[-1][0], pg_d[-1][1]]),
    "rest": float(sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in pg_d[:-1])),
    "last_len": float(np.sqrt(d2d[pg_d[-1][0], pg_d[-1][1]])),
    "opt_worst_len": float(np.sqrt(max(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d))),
}

# Greedy takes the closest available pair every time, so its pick order is
# already ascending and the two matchings can be compared rank by rank.
g_rank = sorted(d2d[i, j] for i, j in pg_d)
o_rank = sorted(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)
demo["n"] = len(g_rank)
demo["g_better"] = int(sum(g < o for g, o in zip(g_rank, o_rank)))
demo["saved"] = float(sum(o - g for g, o in zip(g_rank, o_rank) if g < o))
demo["lost"] = float(sum(g - o for g, o in zip(g_rank, o_rank) if g > o))
```

The obvious way to form pairs is the "greedy" approach: pair the two closest
units anywhere in the sample, then repeat on what is left. It is easy to
explain and implement, but it does not produce the minimum.

Drag the slider to watch it choose. The middle plot shows what each pair
costs, on a log scale because the range is wide, and the bottom panel the
running total. Each plots the optimal matching alongside, both ranked closest
pair first. The early pairs are nearly free, and the
final one costs `{python} f"{demo['last']:.1f}"` against
`{python} f"{demo['rest']:.1f}"` for the other nineteen put together.

```{python}
#| label: greedy-widget
#| echo: false

widget(
    "greedy-steps.js", "gs-demo",
    {
        "pts": np.round(Xd, 4).tolist(),
        "greedy": [[int(i), int(j), round(float(d2d[i, j]), 4)]
                   for i, j in pg_d],
        "optimal": [[int(i), int(j), round(float(d2d[i, j]), 4)]
                    for i, j in po_d],
        "optWorst": float(max(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)),
        "optTotal": float(sum(d2d[i, j] for i, j in po_d)),
        "xlab": "X",
        "ylab": "Y",
        "colors": WIDGET_COLORS,
    },
    """
<style>
.gs-wrap { margin: 1.2rem 0 1.6rem; }
.gs-wrap canvas { display:block; width:100%; touch-action:manipulation; }

</style>

         aria-label="Number of pairs greedy has formed">

  </div>

```

Greedy matching is closer than the optimal matching on
`{python} f"{demo['g_better']}"` of the
`{python} f"{demo['n']}"` ranks, because taking the nearest available pair at
every step collects near-duplicates that the optimal matching gives up. Those
wins come to `{python} f"{demo['saved']:.1f}"` in total, against
`{python} f"{demo['lost']:.1f}"` at the ranks where it loses.

Greedy pairing strands the units it leaves until last. The gap for those last
pairs goes into the variance of the treatment effect estimate, so the tail of
the distance distribution matters more than its total.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the lengths mean here, and what they would mean on real data

Here the sample is rescaled so that $S$ is the identity. The Mahalanobis
distance is then the plain straight-line distance, so each line’s length is
exactly what is being minimised.

Rescaling changes the picture, not the distances: $D^2$ is unchanged by linear
transformations of the covariates.

Real covariates are usually correlated. Then equal distances form tilted
ellipses rather than circles, so screen length no longer tracks distance. A
gap along the long axis is cheap because such differences are common, while
the same gap across the short axis is expensive because that combination is
rare.
:::

The cost of the greedy algorithm over the optimal algorithm depends on the
sample. With 40 units, the greedy algorithm reaches
`{python} f"{demo['mult']:.1f}"` times the optimal total distance and the cost
of the worst pair is `{python} f"{demo['worst']:.0f}"` times greater. Forty
units is a hard case for it, so the table below runs the same comparison at a
few hundred, which is the size this design is usually for.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-greedy
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'Optimal against greedy pairing on the same samples. Greedy loses some of the total, and much more of the worst case.'

rows, gt = [], {}
for N_, p_ in [(100, 4), (200, 4), (200, 8)]:
    Xg = correlated_X(N_, p_, np.random.default_rng(100 + N_ + p_))
    d2g, _, _ = pair_distances(Xg)
    po, pg = optimal_pairs(d2g), greedy_pairs(d2g)
    to = sum(d2g[i, j] for i, j in po)
    tg = sum(d2g[i, j] for i, j in pg)
    mo = max(d2g[i, j] for i, j in po)
    mg = max(d2g[i, j] for i, j in pg)
    rows.append({
        "Sample": f"N = {N_}, k = {p_}",
        "Total D<sup>2</sup>, optimal": f"{to:.1f}",
        "Total D<sup>2</sup>, greedy": f"{tg:.1f} (+{100 * (tg / to - 1):.0f}%)",
        "Worst pair, optimal": f"{mo:.2f}",
        "Worst pair, greedy": f"{mg:.2f} ({mg / mo:.1f}×)",
    })
    gt[(N_, p_)] = {"total": 100 * (tg / to - 1), "worst": mg / mo}
pd.DataFrame(rows).style.hide(axis="index")
```

The two columns move in opposite directions as the sample grows. At
$N = 200$ with four covariates greedy's total is only
`{python} f"{gt[(200, 4)]['total']:.0f}"`% above optimal, against
`{python} f"{100 * (demo['mult'] - 1):.0f}"`% at forty units, so the totals
converge. Its worst pair still costs
`{python} f"{gt[(200, 4)]['worst']:.1f}"` times more, and at eight covariates
`{python} f"{gt[(200, 8)]['worst']:.1f}"` times more. The total becomes a
worse and worse guide to the thing that matters.

Edmonds’ blossom algorithm solves the problem exactly in $O(N^3)$. Because any
unit may pair with any other, the graph is not bipartite and the Hungarian
algorithm does not apply; Greevy et al. (2004) introduced this non-bipartite
form for the design. In Python it is available in networkx and in R through
the nbpMatching package. The button in the bottom right shows the optimal
matching for comparison.

## Odd numbers, and units with nothing close to them

One mechanism solves two awkward cases. A perfect matching needs an
even $N$, so an odd sample leaves a unit over. Separately, a sample may contain
units that sit far from everything else, and forcing them into pairs produces
exactly the stranded pairs the previous section warned about.

Both are solved by adding **sinks**. A sink is a phantom unit placed at
distance zero from every real unit, with no edge to another sink. Because a
sink has to be matched and cannot take another sink, it takes a real unit out
of the experiment. Pairing with a sink is free, so the solver spends its sinks
on whichever units were most expensive to pair.

One sink absorbs the odd unit in an odd sample. Beyond that, sinks come in
pairs: each one removes a real unit, so you need an even number of them to
leave an even number of units behind. Adding two sinks excludes the two units
whose matches would have been worst, four excludes the worst four, and so on.

Drag below to add sinks to a sample containing four units placed well away from
the rest.

```{python}
#| label: sinks-widget
#| echo: false

rng_s = np.random.default_rng(11)
Xs = correlated_X(40, 2, rng_s)
Xs = np.vstack([Xs, np.array([[3.4, 2.9], [-3.1, 2.6],
                              [2.8, -3.2], [0.2, 3.6]])])
Xs = whiten(Xs)              # again, same distances, honest picture
Ns = len(Xs)
d2s, _, _ = pair_distances(Xs)


def match_with_sinks(m):
    G = nx.Graph()
    for i in range(Ns):
        for j in range(i + 1, Ns):
            G.add_edge(i, j, weight=float(d2s[i, j]))
    for s in range(m):
        for i in range(Ns):
            G.add_edge(f"s{s}", i, weight=0.0)
    dropped, prs = [], []
    for a, b in nx.min_weight_matching(G):
        if isinstance(a, str) or isinstance(b, str):
            dropped.append(int(b if isinstance(a, str) else a))
        else:
            prs.append((int(a), int(b)))
    return sorted(dropped), prs


states = []
for m in [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]:
    dropped, prs = match_with_sinks(m)
    assert len(prs) * 2 + len(dropped) == Ns
    states.append({
        "sinks": m,
        "dropped": dropped,
        "pairs": [[i, j, round(float(d2s[i, j]), 4)] for i, j in prs],
        "worst": float(max(d2s[i, j] for i, j in prs)),
        "total": float(sum(d2s[i, j] for i, j in prs)),
    })

# states are [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] sinks, so index 1 is the two-sink case the
# sentence below refers to
sink_drop = 100 * (1 - states[1]["worst"] / states[0]["worst"])

widget(
    "sinks-widget.js", "sk-demo",
    {"pts": np.round(Xs, 4).tolist(), "states": states,
     "xlab": "covariate 1", "colors": WIDGET_COLORS},
    """
<style>
.sk-wrap { margin: 1.2rem 0 1.6rem; }
.sk-wrap canvas { display:block; width:100%; touch-action:manipulation; }
.sk-wrap .sk-readout { font-size:.82rem; color:#5b6570; text-align:center;
  margin:.35rem 0 .6rem; }
.sk-wrap .sk-readout b { color:#21252b; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; }
.sk-wrap .sk-sep { margin:0 .55rem; opacity:.45; }
.sk-wrap input[type=range] { width:100%; margin:0; accent-color:#2c6e9b; }
.sk-wrap .sk-labels { position:relative; height:1.15rem; margin-top:.3rem;
  font-size:.82rem; color:#8a929a; --thumb:16px; }
.sk-wrap .sk-labels span { position:absolute; cursor:pointer;
  white-space:nowrap; transform:translateX(-50%);
  left:calc(var(--thumb) / 2 + var(--p) * (100% - var(--thumb))); }
.sk-wrap .sk-labels span.sk-on { color:#2c4a63; font-weight:600; }
</style>
<div class="sk-wrap" id="sk-demo">
  <canvas></canvas>
  <div class="sk-readout"></div>
  <input type="range" min="0" max="4" step="1" value="0"
         aria-label="Number of sinks added">
  <div class="sk-labels">
    <span style="--p:0">0</span><span style="--p:.25">2</span><span
      style="--p:.5">4</span><span style="--p:.75">6</span><span
      style="--p:1">8</span>
  </div>
</div>
""")
```

The first two sinks remove the two worst-placed units and the worst remaining
pair falls by `{python} f"{sink_drop:.0f}"`%. Two more remove the rest of the
awkward group. After that the returns shrink, and every further sink costs real
sample size.

A **caliper** sets a maximum acceptable within-pair distance. Implementing one
by raising the weight of long edges can leave a problem with no feasible
solution, so the usual route is a caliper enforced through sinks: make a sink
cheaper than any pairing beyond the cap, and units with no acceptable partner
drop out by themselves. Every unit you exclude narrows what the experiment
covers, so record how many and which ones.

## Analysing a matched experiment

The point estimate needs no special treatment. Averaging the within-pair
differences and taking the plain difference in group means are the same
arithmetic, because every pair puts one unit in each arm. There is no way to
forget the matching when forming the estimate.

```{python}
#| label: se-setup
#| include: false

y_nl, r2_nl, _ = make_y("nonlinear", np.random.default_rng(3))

Y = y_nl[None, :] + 0.0 * T_pm
mt = np.where(T_pm, Y, np.nan)
mc = np.where(T_pm, np.nan, Y)
est_pm = np.nanmean(mt, 1) - np.nanmean(mc, 1)
se_unpaired = np.sqrt(np.nanvar(mt, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2)
                      + np.nanvar(mc, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2))

first_is_t = T_pm[:, i0]
wdiff = np.where(first_is_t, Y[:, i0] - Y[:, i1], Y[:, i1] - Y[:, i0])
se_paired = wdiff.std(1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(nP)

tc_un = stats.t.ppf(0.975, N - 2)
tc_pr = stats.t.ppf(0.975, nP - 1)
cov_un = (np.abs(est_pm) <= tc_un * se_unpaired).mean()
cov_pr = (np.abs(est_pm) <= tc_pr * se_paired).mean()
sd_true = est_pm.std(ddof=1)
```

A two-sample $t$-test computes the standard error from the within-arm
variances. Under this design each arm contains one unit from every pair, so
each arm spans the full covariate range and its variance is close to the
variance of the whole sample. That calculation returns roughly the value it
would have returned under plain randomisation, while the estimate itself now
moves around far less. The interval comes out
`{python} f"{100 * (se_unpaired.mean() / sd_true - 1):.0f}"`% too wide, and
covers the true effect
`{python} f"{100 * cov_un:.1f}"`% of the time instead of 95%.

Differencing within pairs fixes it. The within-pair difference is the unit of
analysis, and its spread already reflects how closely the pairs were matched,
so the interval lands at `{python} f"{100 * cov_pr:.1f}"`% coverage. A
regression of the outcome on treatment plus a fixed effect for each pair is the
same calculation and gives the same standard error. The cost is degrees of
freedom, $N/2 - 1$ rather than $N - 2$, which is minor at a few hundred units.

The upper bound on what this is worth is set by the covariates. For a perfectly
matched sample the variance of the estimate falls to the share of outcome
variance the covariates do not explain, so the naive variance is too large by
at most $1/(1 - R^2)$ and the naive standard error by at most
$1/\sqrt{1 - R^2}$. Here $R^2$ is `{python} f"{r2_nl:.2f}"`, giving a ceiling
of `{python} f"{1 / np.sqrt(1 - r2_nl):.2f}"` on the standard error against the
`{python} f"{se_unpaired.mean() / sd_true:.2f}"` realised, so the matching
captured
`{python} f"{100 * (1 - sd_true ** 2 / se_unpaired.mean() ** 2) / r2_nl:.0f}"`%
of what a perfect matching would have removed.

### A conservative interval is not always a safe one

Conservative is accurate but incomplete: lost precision is not the only
consequence.

```{python}
#| label: fig-power
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: 'Rejection rate of a two-sided 5% test against the size of the true effect, on the same sample and the same 4,000 assignments. At a true effect of zero the rejection rate is the false positive rate, which should be 5%. Below an effect of about 0.35 the matched design analysed without the pairing is less powerful than not matching at all.'

taus = np.linspace(0, 0.6, 25)
pw_cr, pw_un, pw_pr = [], [], []
for tau in taus:
    Yc = y_nl[None, :] + tau * T_cr
    a_ = np.where(T_cr, Yc, np.nan)
    b_ = np.where(T_cr, np.nan, Yc)
    e_c = np.nanmean(a_, 1) - np.nanmean(b_, 1)
    s_c = np.sqrt(np.nanvar(a_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2)
                  + np.nanvar(b_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2))
    pw_cr.append((np.abs(e_c / s_c) > tc_un).mean())

    Yp = y_nl[None, :] + tau * T_pm
    a_ = np.where(T_pm, Yp, np.nan)
    b_ = np.where(T_pm, np.nan, Yp)
    e_p = np.nanmean(a_, 1) - np.nanmean(b_, 1)
    s_u = np.sqrt(np.nanvar(a_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2)
                  + np.nanvar(b_, 1, ddof=1) / (N // 2))
    wd = np.where(T_pm[:, i0], Yp[:, i0] - Yp[:, i1], Yp[:, i1] - Yp[:, i0])
    s_p = wd.std(1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(nP)
    pw_un.append((np.abs(e_p / s_u) > tc_un).mean())
    pw_pr.append((np.abs(e_p / s_p) > tc_pr).mean())

pw_cr, pw_un, pw_pr = (100 * np.array(v) for v in (pw_cr, pw_un, pw_pr))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
series = [(pw_pr, "Matched, within-pair SE", C["blue"], "-"),
          (pw_cr, "Plain randomisation", C["grey"], "-"),
          (pw_un, "Matched, two-sample SE", C["red"], "--")]
for v, lab, col, ls in series:
    ax.plot(taus, v, color=col, lw=2.0, ls=ls, label=lab, zorder=3)

ax.axhline(5, color="#b9c0c7", lw=1, ls=":", zorder=1)

# the zero-effect end is the false positive rate, so call it out
for v, _, col, _ in series:
    ax.plot([0], [v[0]], "o", color=col, ms=6, zorder=5,
            markeredgecolor="white", markeredgewidth=1.2)
# the band between the curves and the top annotation is empty out to about
# x = 0.2, so the note sits there rather than across the rising lines
ax.annotate(f"at no true effect:\n{pw_pr[0]:.0f}% and {pw_cr[0]:.0f}% are "
            f"correct,\n{pw_un[0]:.0f}% is over-cautious",
            xy=(0.004, 6.5), xytext=(0.012, 46), fontsize=8.2,
            color="#3f4850", ha="left", va="top",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="#9aa4ad", lw=1))

# where the two lower curves actually meet, interpolated rather than snapped
# to the next grid point
gap = pw_un - pw_cr
k = int(np.argmax(gap >= 0))
cross = (taus[k] if k == 0
         else float(np.interp(0.0, [gap[k - 1], gap[k]], [taus[k - 1], taus[k]])))

ax.axvline(cross, color="#9aa4ad", lw=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.008, 99), xytext=(cross, 99),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#6b747c", lw=1.3,
                            shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
ax.text(0.015, 94.5,
        "between zero and this line, a matched\n"
        "design analysed with a two-sample SE\n"
        "rejects less often than not matching",
        fontsize=8.2, color="#6b747c", va="top", ha="left")

ax.set_xlabel("true treatment effect")
ax.set_ylabel("rejection rate (%)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 103)
ax.set_xlim(-0.012, 0.62)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(color="#eef1f4", zorder=0)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read the dashed red line against the grey one. The matched design analysed
with a two-sample standard error rejects less often than plain randomisation
does. At a true effect of zero that is what you want, because the rejection
rate there is the false positive rate. Above zero it is lost power, until the
ordering reverses once the effect is large enough. A test statistic that is
both smaller in spread and centred below the critical value crosses that value
less often, so the tighter estimate works against you until the effect clears
the bar on its own.
Bruhn and McKenzie report the same effect: failing to account for the
randomisation method gives tests of the wrong size, and can give less power
than a plain random draw would have.

The blue line is what the design was for.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The pairing has to survive to the analysis
Matching moves its gain into the analysis stage, where it needs the pair labels
to claim it. If the data reaches you aggregated, say a count and a sum per arm
per day, the pair structure is gone and the only standard error you can compute
is the conservative one. Store the pair identifier alongside the assignment at
the point you randomise, and carry it through every table that follows.

Rerandomization does not share this exposure, because a strict threshold banks
most of its gain at the design stage. If you know the analysis will run on
aggregates, that is a point in favour of a threshold over pairs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to do
Pair on the covariates you have reason to believe predict the outcome, solve
the matching exactly, keep the pair identifier, and analyse within pairs.
Matching on covariates that do not predict the outcome spends degrees of
freedom and returns nothing.
:::
